name: INTERCAL
title: INTERCAL, politely
intro: INTERCAL was written in 1972 by Don Woods and James Lyon to be unlike every other language. It has no ordinary arithmetic operators, judges your manners, and prints numbers in Roman numerals. It is a joke, but a carefully built one, and reading it shows how much we take for granted in normal languages. C-INTERCAL (the ick compiler) runs it today.

lessons.title: Statements and manners
lessons.summary: DO, PLEASE, variables and Roman numerals.

sections.p: Every statement starts with DO, PLEASE or PLEASE DO. The compiler counts your manners: if fewer than about one statement in five says PLEASE it refuses the program as impolite, and if more than about one in three does, it refuses it as overly polite. The program ends with GIVE UP.
sections.code:
DO .1 <- #5
DO .2 <- #3
PLEASE READ OUT .1
DO GIVE UP

sections.p: Names are a symbol and a number. .1 is a 16-bit variable (a “spot”), :1 is 32-bit (a “two-spot”), and ,1 and ;1 are arrays. Constants start with a mesh: #5. Assignment is <-.

READ OUT prints a number as Roman numerals, so the program above prints V. Large numbers use a bar over the letters to mean thousands. WRITE IN reads numbers typed as English digit names, such as ONE FIVE for 15.

There is no plus or minus. Instead there are two binary operators, mingle ($, which interleaves the bits of two numbers) and select (~, which picks bits out of one number using another as a mask), plus unary AND, OR and XOR (&, V, ?) that work on neighbouring bits of a single number. Arithmetic is done by calling library routines with NEXT.

Instead of GOTO, INTERCAL has COME FROM (10): when the line labelled (10) finishes, control jumps to the COME FROM. It began as a parody of GOTO and has since been borrowed seriously for debuggers and aspect-oriented ideas.

practice.q: What does READ OUT print for the value 5?
practice.answer: V
practice.why: INTERCAL output uses Roman numerals.

practice.q: Which is a 32-bit variable?
practice.why: The two-spot (:) marks a 32-bit variable; one spot (.) is 16-bit; # is a constant.

practice.q: What happens if no statement says PLEASE?
options: The compiler rejects the program as impolite
practice.answer: The compiler rejects the program as impolite
practice.why: Too little politeness, and too much, are both errors.

practice.q: How is the constant 3 written?
practice.why: Constants start with the mesh symbol #.

practice.q: What does COME FROM (10) do?
options: Jumps to itself after line (10) runs
practice.answer: Jumps to itself after line (10) runs
practice.why: It is GOTO turned around: the jump is declared at the destination.

practice.q: How does a program end?
practice.answer: DO GIVE UP
practice.why: GIVE UP is the polite way to finish; there is no END or STOP.

practice.q: What is .1?
practice.answer: A 16-bit variable (a spot)
practice.why: One spot (.) is 16-bit; two-spot (:) is 32-bit; mesh (#) is a constant.

practice.q: How do you type the number 15 for WRITE IN?
practice.answer: ONE FIVE
practice.why: WRITE IN reads English digit names, not digits or Roman numerals.

practice.q: What happens if too many statements say PLEASE?
options: The compiler rejects the program as overly polite
practice.answer: The compiler rejects the program as overly polite
practice.why: About one PLEASE in three to five is the safe band; more is rejected.

lessons.title: Mingle and select
lessons.summary: The two binary operators, worked out bit by bit.

sections.p: Mingle ($, also written as a c with a line through it, the “change” sign) takes two 16-bit values and interleaves their bits into one 32-bit value. The left value's bits land in the odd positions and the right value's in the even ones, starting from the right. The lines that begin DO NOTE are comments: INTERCAL reads them as DO NOT E…, a statement switched off for good.
sections.code:
DO NOTE #3 $ #0
DO NOTE left  #3 = 11 in binary
DO NOTE right #0 = 00
DO NOTE interleave left, right, left, right = 1 0 1 0
DO NOTE 1010 in binary is 10
DO :1 <- #3 $ #0

sections.p: Select (~) uses the right value as a mask. It picks out the bits of the left value where the mask has a 1, and packs them together at the right-hand end. The manual's own example is #179 ~ #201: 179 is 10110011, the mask 201 is 11001001, the picked bits are 1, 0, 0 and 1, and 1001 is 9.
sections.code:
DO NOTE #179 ~ #201
DO NOTE 179  = 1 0 1 1 0 0 1 1
DO NOTE 201  = 1 1 0 0 1 0 0 1   (mask)
DO NOTE kept = 1 0 . . 0 . . 1   gives 1001, which is 9
DO .1 <- #179 ~ #201

sections.p: Together mingle and select can do anything: mingle builds wide values, select pulls bits back out, and a mask of all ones (#65535) selects a whole 16-bit value. They are just very inconvenient on purpose, which is why real INTERCAL programs lean on the system library for arithmetic.

practice.q: What is #1 $ #0?
practice.why: The left value's bit 0 goes to position 1, so the result is binary 10, which is 2.

practice.q: What is #0 $ #1?
practice.why: The right value's bits take the even positions, so its bit 0 stays at position 0.

practice.q: What is #2 $ #3?
practice.why: Left 10 and right 11 interleave to 1 1 0 1, which is 13.

practice.q: What is #12 ~ #7?
practice.why: The mask 0111 keeps the low three bits of 1100, which are 100: 4.

practice.q: What is #6 ~ #6?
practice.why: The mask 110 keeps two bits of 110, both 1, packed as 11: 3.

practice.q: What is #1 $ #1?
practice.why: Left and right each contribute bit 0, interleaved as binary 11.

practice.q: What is #3 $ #0?
practice.why: Left 11 and right 00 interleave to 1010, which is 10 — the manual's style of example.

practice.q: What is #15 ~ #10?
practice.why: Mask 1010 keeps bits 1 and 3 of 1111, both 1, packed as 11: 3.

practice.q: What is #8 ~ #8?
practice.why: The mask keeps only the high 1 of 1000, packed down to bit 0.

practice.q: What does a mask of #65535 do in a select?
practice.answer: Selects a whole 16-bit value
practice.why: All ones in the mask keep every bit, packed as the original 16-bit number.

lessons.title: The unary operators
lessons.summary: AND, OR and XOR of a number with itself, rotated.

sections.p: The unary operators & (AND), V (OR) and ? (XOR) take one value. They rotate it one bit to the right (the lowest bit wraps round to the top) and combine each bit with the rotated copy. The operator is written inside the name, after the spot or mesh: .&1, #V77.
INTERCAL has no brackets. Instead, sparks (') and rabbit ears (") group sub-expressions, and they can be nested by alternating them. Reading which spark matches which is part of the fun.

practice.q: What does the unary & combine each bit with?
options: The bit to its left, wrapping round
The bit to its right only
The same bit of another number
practice.answer: The bit to its left, wrapping round
practice.why: The value is rotated right by one, so each bit meets its left-hand neighbour; the top bit meets the lowest.

practice.q: What is &#3?
practice.why: 3 is ...011; the two low bits are both 1, so AND keeps one 1 at the bottom, and the wrapped top pair gives 0: result 1.

practice.q: What is &#5?
practice.why: 5 is 101: no two neighbouring bits are both 1, so AND gives 0.

practice.q: What groups part of an expression in INTERCAL?
practice.answer: Sparks ' and rabbit ears "
practice.why: There are no brackets; sparks and rabbit ears do the job and alternate when nested.

practice.q: What is &#7?
practice.why: 7 is ...0111; AND with its right-rotate keeps the low two bits as 11: 3.

practice.q: What is &#1?
practice.why: The single 1 meets the wrapped 0 from the top, so AND clears it.

practice.q: Where is a unary operator written?
options: Inside the name, after the spot or mesh
Only at the start of a line
practice.answer: Inside the name, after the spot or mesh
practice.why: Forms like .&1 and #V77 put &, V or ? inside the variable or constant.

practice.q: What does unary V do?
options: OR of each bit with its left-hand neighbour
practice.answer: OR of each bit with its left-hand neighbour
practice.why: V is unary OR against the right-rotated copy; & is AND and ? is XOR.

lessons.title: NEXT, RESUME and FORGET
lessons.summary: Calling, returning and the NEXT stack.

sections.p: Lines can carry a label in brackets, such as (10). DO (10) NEXT jumps to line (10) and remembers where it came from on the NEXT stack, which holds at most 79 entries. DO RESUME #1 goes back one entry; DO FORGET #1 throws one entry away without going back. A program that fills the stack dies with an error, so every NEXT needs a matching RESUME or FORGET.
sections.code:
DO (10) NEXT
        DO READ OUT .1
        DO GIVE UP
(10)    DO .1 <- #7
        PLEASE RESUME #1

sections.p: Adding two numbers is a library call. Put the values in .1 and .2, call (1000), and the sum appears in .3. The system library also subtracts, multiplies and divides, all written in INTERCAL itself out of mingles and selects.
sections.code:
DO .1 <- #2
DO .2 <- #3
PLEASE DO (1000) NEXT
DO READ OUT .3

sections.p: There is no IF. A classic trick computes #1 or #2 from a test, then does RESUME by that amount: resuming by 1 returns normally, resuming by 2 skips back one level further. It is as hard to read as it sounds, which is the point.

practice.q: What does DO (10) NEXT do?
options: Jumps to (10) and remembers where it came from
practice.answer: Jumps to (10) and remembers where it came from
practice.why: NEXT is INTERCAL's call; the return point goes on the NEXT stack.

practice.q: How many entries can the NEXT stack hold?
practice.why: The 80th NEXT is an error.

practice.q: What is the difference between RESUME #1 and FORGET #1?
options: RESUME returns to the saved place; FORGET drops it and carries on
practice.answer: RESUME returns to the saved place; FORGET drops it and carries on
practice.why: Both remove an entry; only RESUME jumps to it.

practice.q: Where does (1000) put the sum of .1 and .2?
practice.why: The library routine leaves its answer in .3.

practice.q: How is a line labelled?
options: A number in brackets before the statement
practice.answer: A number in brackets before the statement
practice.why: Labels look like (10) at the start of the line.

practice.q: What must every NEXT have?
options: A PLEASE on the same line
practice.answer: A matching RESUME or FORGET
practice.why: Otherwise the NEXT stack fills and the program dies.

practice.q: What does RESUME #2 do compared with RESUME #1?
options: Returns two levels up the NEXT stack
Returns twice as far in the file
practice.answer: Returns two levels up the NEXT stack
practice.why: The number is how many stack entries to pop while returning; 2 is a classic conditional trick.

practice.q: Where do you put the addends before calling (1000)?
practice.answer: In .1 and .2
practice.why: The system library reads .1 and .2 and leaves the sum in .3.

lessons.title: ABSTAIN, STASH and chance
lessons.summary: Switching statements off, saving variables and percentages.

sections.p: DO ABSTAIN FROM (20) switches line (20) off; DO REINSTATE (20) switches it back on. You can also abstain from a kind of statement: DO ABSTAIN FROM READING OUT silences every output. A statement written with NOT or N'T (DON'T, PLEASE DON'T) starts switched off.
sections.code:
DO ABSTAIN FROM (20)
(20)    PLEASE READ OUT #1
        DO REINSTATE (20)
        DO GIVE UP

sections.p: DO STASH .1 saves a copy of .1 on its own private stack; DO RETRIEVE .1 brings the saved value back. It is how routines keep the caller's variables safe. IGNORE makes a variable read-only until REMEMBER.
sections.code:
DO .1 <- #5
DO STASH .1
DO .1 <- #9
DO RETRIEVE .1
PLEASE READ OUT .1

sections.p: A statement can start with a percentage, such as DO %50 READ OUT .1, meaning it runs with that chance each time. INTERCAL may be the only language where randomness is a statement prefix.

practice.q: What does DON'T at the start of a statement mean?
options: The statement is a comment and can never run
practice.answer: The statement starts switched off
practice.why: It is abstained from at the start; REINSTATE can switch it on later.

practice.q: After DO .1 <- #5, DO STASH .1, DO .1 <- #9, DO RETRIEVE .1, what is in .1?
practice.why: RETRIEVE brings back the value that was stashed.

practice.q: What does DO %25 READ OUT .1 do?
options: Prints .1 about one time in four
practice.answer: Prints .1 about one time in four
practice.why: The percentage is the chance that the statement runs.

practice.q: What does DO ABSTAIN FROM READING OUT do?
options: Switches off every READ OUT statement
practice.answer: Switches off every READ OUT statement
practice.why: Abstaining by gerund affects every statement of that kind.

practice.q: What does DO REINSTATE (20) do?
practice.answer: Switches line (20) back on
practice.why: REINSTATE undoes an ABSTAIN for that label.

practice.q: What does IGNORE do to a variable?
practice.answer: Makes it read-only until REMEMBER
practice.why: Assignments are ignored while the variable is IGNOREd.

practice.q: Where does STASH keep the saved value?
options: On that variable's own private stack
practice.answer: On that variable's own private stack
practice.why: Each variable has its own stash; RETRIEVE pops it back.

practice.q: How does DO NOTE… become a comment?
options: It is read as DO NOT E…, a statement switched off
NOTE is a reserved comment keyword
The compiler strips lines starting with N
practice.answer: It is read as DO NOT E…, a statement switched off
practice.why: NOT / N'T abstains the statement for good, so DO NOTE… never runs.

sections.p: A tail (,1) is a 16-bit array; a hybrid (;1) is a 32-bit array. You create one by assigning a dimension: DO ,1 <- #3 makes ,1 three elements long. Elements are written ,1 SUB #1 (the first element is #1, not zero). Reading or writing past the dimension is an error.
sections.code:
DO ,1 <- #3
DO ,1 SUB #1 <- #5
DO ,1 SUB #2 <- #10
DO ,1 SUB #3 <- #15
PLEASE READ OUT ,1 SUB #2
DO GIVE UP

sections.p: The program above prints X — Roman for 10. Arrays are how INTERCAL stores tables and buffers; the system library uses them heavily. Multidimensional arrays exist too: DO ,1 <- #2 BY #3 is a 2×3 tail, indexed with two SUBs.
DO STASH ,1 saves the whole array (dimension and contents) on that array’s private stack; RETRIEVE brings it back. Routines that need a scratch buffer stash the caller’s array first.

practice.q: What is ,1?
practice.answer: A 16-bit array (a tail)
practice.why: The single spot with a comma marks a tail; semicolon is a hybrid.

practice.q: What does DO ,1 <- #3 do?
practice.answer: Creates ,1 with three elements
practice.why: Assigning a mesh to an array name sets its dimension.

practice.q: How is the first element of ,1 written?
practice.answer: ,1 SUB #1
practice.why: INTERCAL arrays are 1-based; SUB picks the element.

practice.q: What does the sample print?
practice.answer: X
practice.why: Element 2 holds 10, and READ OUT uses Roman numerals.

practice.q: What is ;1?
practice.answer: A 32-bit array (a hybrid)
practice.why: Semicolon marks hybrids; colon alone is a two-spot scalar.

practice.q: What does DO ,1 <- #2 BY #3 create?
practice.answer: A 2×3 multidimensional tail
practice.why: BY adds another dimension; two SUBs index it.

practice.q: What does STASH ,1 save?
options: The whole array’s dimension and contents
practice.answer: The whole array’s dimension and contents
practice.why: Array stash is complete; RETRIEVE restores both size and values.

practice.q: What happens if you write ,1 SUB #4 after DO ,1 <- #3?
practice.answer: An error: past the dimension
practice.why: The dimension is fixed until you reassign the array name.

lessons.title: COME FROM in depth
lessons.summary: Labels that pull, and computed destinations.

sections.p: COME FROM (10) sits at the destination: when labelled line (10) finishes, control is pulled to the COME FROM. Several COME FROMs aimed at the same label are an error unless all but one are abstained. That is how INTERCAL turns “who jumps here?” into a question you answer at the landing site.
sections.code:
(10)    DO .1 <- #1
        DO READ OUT .1
        PLEASE GIVE UP
        DO COME FROM (10)
        DO .1 <- #2
        DO READ OUT .1
        DO GIVE UP

sections.p: C-INTERCAL allows COME FROM .1: the destination label is the current value of .1. Change the variable and the same statement pulls from a different line. It is as bewildering as it sounds, and it is a favourite of the language’s fans.

NEXT pushes a return address; COME FROM does not. Mixing them is legal but easy to misread: a COME FROM can yank you out of a routine before RESUME runs, leaving a stale NEXT-stack entry unless you FORGET.

practice.q: Where is COME FROM written?
options: At the destination that should receive control
At the line you want to leave
practice.answer: At the destination that should receive control
practice.why: The jump is declared where you land, not where you leave.

practice.q: When does COME FROM (10) fire?
practice.answer: After the statement labelled (10) finishes
practice.why: Finishing the labelled line pulls control to the COME FROM.

practice.q: What if two active COME FROMs target the same label?
practice.answer: An error
practice.why: Only one active pull per label is allowed; ABSTAIN the extras.

practice.q: What is COME FROM .1?
options: A computed COME FROM whose label is the value of .1
A syntax error in every INTERCAL
practice.answer: A computed COME FROM whose label is the value of .1
practice.why: C-INTERCAL lets the destination come from a variable.

practice.q: Does COME FROM push the NEXT stack?
practice.answer: No
practice.why: COME FROM is not a call. NEXT is the one that remembers a return.

practice.q: Why can COME FROM upset a NEXT/RESUME pair?
options: It can yank control away before RESUME, leaving a stale stack entry
It cannot; they ignore each other
practice.answer: It can yank control away before RESUME, leaving a stale stack entry
practice.why: A pull mid-routine skips the matching RESUME unless you FORGET.

practice.q: How do you keep a spare COME FROM without using it?
options: ABSTAIN from it (or write it with DON'T)
practice.answer: ABSTAIN from it (or write it with DON'T)
practice.why: An abstained COME FROM does not pull, so another may target the same label.

practice.q: In the sample, after (10) runs, where does control go?
options: To the COME FROM, which then sets .1 to 2 and prints II
Straight to GIVE UP, printing only I
Back to the top of the file
Nowhere; COME FROM is a comment
practice.answer: To the COME FROM, which then sets .1 to 2 and prints II
practice.why: The first GIVE UP is skipped because COME FROM pulls first; .1 becomes 2.

lessons.title: IGNORE and REMEMBER
lessons.summary: Read-only variables until you remember them.

sections.p: DO IGNORE .1 makes assignments to .1 silently fail: the value stays put. DO REMEMBER .1 turns writing back on. Reads still work while a variable is ignored. The feature exists so a routine can protect the caller’s registers without stashing everything.
sections.code:
DO .1 <- #5
DO IGNORE .1
DO .1 <- #9
PLEASE READ OUT .1
DO REMEMBER .1
DO .1 <- #3
PLEASE READ OUT .1
DO GIVE UP

sections.p: The first READ OUT prints V (still 5); the second prints III (3). The assignment of 9 was ignored. You can ignore several variables in one statement: DO IGNORE .1 + .2 + :1.

Ignoring an array freezes every element and the dimension. Trying to resize it with DO ,1 <- #10 does nothing while ,1 is ignored. STASH / RETRIEVE still work: they are not assignments through the ignored path.

practice.q: After IGNORE .1, what does DO .1 <- #9 do?
practice.answer: Leaves .1 unchanged
practice.why: Ignored variables refuse writes; the old value remains.

practice.q: What does the sample print?
practice.answer: V then III
practice.why: 9 never sticks; after REMEMBER, 3 does.

practice.q: What does REMEMBER do?
practice.answer: Allows assignments again
practice.why: REMEMBER undoes IGNORE for those names.

practice.q: Can you still READ OUT an ignored variable?
practice.answer: Yes; only writes are blocked
practice.why: IGNORE is write protection, not invisibility.

practice.q: How do you ignore .1 and .2 together?
practice.answer: DO IGNORE .1 + .2
practice.why: A plus list names several targets in one IGNORE or REMEMBER.

practice.q: While ,1 is ignored, what does DO ,1 <- #10 do?
options: Nothing; the dimension stays as it was
practice.answer: Nothing; the dimension stays as it was
practice.why: Resizing is an assignment to the array name, so IGNORE blocks it.

practice.q: Why use IGNORE instead of STASH?
options: To freeze a value in place without copying it to a stash stack
practice.answer: To freeze a value in place without copying it to a stash stack
practice.why: IGNORE protects in situ; STASH saves a snapshot you can restore later.

practice.q: Does STASH still work on an ignored variable?
practice.answer: Yes
practice.why: Stashing is not an ordinary assignment of a new value through the ignored write path.

lessons.title: ONCE and AGAIN
lessons.summary: Statements that flip themselves after they run.

sections.p: A statement may end with ONCE or AGAIN. DO … ONCE runs, then abstains itself — the next pass skips it until something REINSTATEs it. DO … AGAIN does the opposite dance with reinstate/abstain so a line can toggle on and off each time control reaches it. Together with ABSTAIN, they are INTERCAL’s idea of a flip-flop.
sections.code:
(20)    PLEASE DO READ OUT .1 ONCE
        DO .1 <- #2
        DO COME FROM (20)
        DO GIVE UP

sections.p: Suppose .1 starts at 1. The first visit to (20) prints I, then the ONCE abstains that READ OUT. The COME FROM loops back, .1 becomes 2, but the output line stays dark. Without ONCE, the loop would print forever.

AGAIN is the sibling that reinstate-toggles. Exact compiler behaviour varies slightly between INTERCAL-72 and C-INTERCAL quirks modes; the safe lesson is that both keywords attach to a single statement and change whether that statement remains active after it runs.

practice.q: What does ONCE do after the statement runs?
options: Abstains that statement so a later pass skips it
Deletes the line from the file
practice.answer: Abstains that statement so a later pass skips it
practice.why: ONCE is a self-ABSTAIN after success.

practice.q: How do you turn a ONCE-abstained line back on?
practice.answer: REINSTATE it
practice.why: ONCE left it abstained; REINSTATE clears that.

practice.q: What is AGAIN for?
options: Toggling a statement’s abstained state across visits
Repeating the next line ten times
practice.answer: Toggling a statement’s abstained state across visits
practice.why: AGAIN is the flip-flop partner of ONCE.

practice.q: In the sample loop, how many times does READ OUT fire?
practice.answer: Once
practice.why: ONCE abstains the print after the first time; COME FROM still loops but stays quiet.

practice.q: Where is ONCE written?
options: At the end of the statement it affects
Only in the compiler command line
practice.answer: At the end of the statement it affects
practice.why: ONCE and AGAIN are suffixes on a single statement.

practice.q: How do ONCE and ABSTAIN FROM relate?
options: ONCE is a self-ABSTAIN after the statement succeeds
ONCE deletes ABSTAIN from the language
practice.answer: ONCE is a self-ABSTAIN after the statement succeeds
practice.why: Same abstain mechanism; different trigger.

practice.q: Why combine ONCE with COME FROM?
options: To run setup once, then loop without repeating that setup
practice.answer: To run setup once, then loop without repeating that setup
practice.why: A classic pattern: initialise on the first pull, then stay in the loop body.

practice.q: Does ONCE affect other statements on later lines?
options: No; only the statement it suffixes
practice.answer: No; only the statement it suffixes
practice.why: The suffix is local to that statement.

lessons.title: The system library
lessons.summary: More arithmetic through NEXT, and where answers land.

sections.p: Beyond addition at (1000), the system library (the standard “syslib”) offers subtraction, multiplication, division and other bit-twiddling routines, all written in INTERCAL. You load arguments into the documented spots, NEXT to the entry label, and read the result from the documented destination — often .3 or :3.
sections.code:
DO .1 <- #10
DO .2 <- #3
PLEASE DO (1009) NEXT
DO READ OUT .3
DO GIVE UP

sections.p: Exact label numbers depend on which syslib you link (INTERCAL-72 versus C-INTERCAL’s expanded library). The pattern does not: arguments in, NEXT, answer out, and a matching RESUME inside the library so your NEXT stack stays balanced. On overflow or divide-by-zero the library may abstain your next statement or set an error indicator — read the syslib commentary for the routine you call.
You can build addition from mingles and selects; the library already did. Real programs call it and save their sanity for the problem at hand — or for arranging enough PLEASEs.

practice.q: Where do you usually put two 16-bit operands for a syslib call?
practice.answer: In .1 and .2
practice.why: The common convention is .1 and .2 in, result in .3 or :3.

practice.q: How do you enter a library routine?
practice.answer: DO (label) NEXT
practice.why: Library entry points are ordinary labelled routines reached by NEXT.

practice.q: Who writes the RESUME that returns from syslib?
options: The COME FROM at the top of the file
practice.answer: The library routine itself
practice.why: A well-behaved routine RESUMEs back to you; your NEXT stack stays balanced.

practice.q: Why do programs call syslib instead of hand-mingling addition?
options: The library already built arithmetic out of mingle and select
Roman numerals only work inside syslib
practice.answer: The library already built arithmetic out of mingle and select
practice.why: Reuse beats re-deriving 16-bit add from bit ops for every program.

practice.q: What should you check when linking a different syslib?
options: The entry labels and where results are left
Whether READ OUT still uses Roman numerals
practice.answer: The entry labels and where results are left
practice.why: Label numbers and register conventions can differ between library versions.

practice.q: In the sample, .1 is 10 and .2 is 3. What kind of answer is .3 meant to hold?
options: The result of the library routine you called
practice.answer: The result of the library routine you called
practice.why: Whatever (1009) implements, its documented destination is .3 here.

practice.q: What can a library do on divide-by-zero or overflow?
options: Abstain your next statement or set an error indicator
practice.answer: Abstain your next statement or set an error indicator
practice.why: Syslib signals failure in INTERCAL-ish ways; read the routine’s notes.

practice.q: Does calling syslib excuse you from PLEASE quotas?
options: No; politeness still applies to your program text
Yes; library calls are always polite enough
practice.answer: No; politeness still applies to your program text
practice.why: The compiler still counts PLEASE in your source.

lessons.title: Project: a polite nut tally
lessons.summary: Arrays, library add, ONCE setup and Roman output.

sections.p: Three nut counts live in a tail. A one-shot setup fills them; a small loop uses the system adder at (1000) to total the elements, then READ OUT prints the sum in Roman numerals. Politeness is spaced through the program so the compiler accepts it. Nothing here is executed by the Programming Learner checker — C-INTERCAL’s ick is the real runner — but the shape is a complete INTERCAL sketch: arrays, NEXT, ONCE and manners.
sections.code:
DO ,1 <- #3
        DO ,1 SUB #1 <- #4
        DO ,1 SUB #2 <- #7
        DO ,1 SUB #3 <- #2
        DO .4 <- #0
        DO .5 <- #1
(10)    PLEASE DO .1 <- .4
        DO .2 <- ,1 SUB .5
        DO (1000) NEXT
        DO .4 <- .3
        DO .5 <- #1 $.5
        DO NOTE .5 steps 1, then 2, then something past 3 — stop early
        DO .6 <- .5 ~ #3
        DO .6 <- #1 $.6
        PLEASE DO (20) NEXT
        DO COME FROM (10)
(20)    DO FORGET #1
        DO READ OUT .4
        DO GIVE UP
        DON'T COME FROM (10)

sections.p: The loop body adds ,1 SUB .5 into a running total in .4. The control logic is deliberately awkward — classic INTERCAL — and the DON'T COME FROM shows a spare pull left abstained. On a real ick, simplify the loop with a clearer ONCE setup and a library compare if your syslib provides one; the printed total for 4+7+2 should be XIII.
Abstain the READ OUT until the loop finishes, stash the array before a destructive pass, or drive the three counts from WRITE IN so a human types FOUR, SEVEN and TWO.

practice.q: What is the sum of the three tail elements in the sketch?
practice.why: 4 + 7 + 2 = 13, which READ OUT would show as XIII.

practice.q: Where does (1000) leave the sum of .1 and .2?
practice.why: The standard adder returns in .3; the sketch copies it into .4.

practice.q: What does DO ,1 <- #3 do at the start?
options: Dimensions the nut-count array to three elements
practice.answer: Dimensions the nut-count array to three elements
practice.why: Assigning a mesh to a tail sets its length.

practice.q: Why does the program include PLEASE on some lines?
options: So the politeness ratio stays in the band the compiler accepts
PLEASE is required before every NEXT
Without PLEASE, arrays do not work
practice.answer: So the politeness ratio stays in the band the compiler accepts
practice.why: Too few or too many PLEASE lines are both compile errors.

practice.q: What is the DON'T COME FROM for?
options: An abstained spare pull, showing a line that does not fire
practice.answer: An abstained spare pull, showing a line that does not fire
practice.why: DON'T starts the statement abstained; it documents an alternate path left off.

practice.q: Why is this course’s checker not running the sketch?
options: INTERCAL needs ick (or similar); the pack has no runner
The sketch has no GIVE UP
practice.answer: INTERCAL needs ick (or similar); the pack has no runner
practice.why: Like Chisel, this pack teaches with static examples and quizzes.

practice.q: What does the running total live in?
practice.why: Each adder result in .3 is copied into .4 for the next round.

practice.q: What would READ OUT print for the final total 13?
practice.answer: XIII
